open-question.question: Git gives up on `.git/index.lock` at once when another process holds it, two runs' writes in one tree land within a second of each other, and a lock left by a crashed process must surface as git's message rather than as a call that waits forever, so the attempt count and the pause between attempts together fix how long a write waits. How many times does a failed git write repeat, and with what pause between attempts?

The retry has to appear in the commit procedure's prose, which eleven skills follow as their own tool calls, and literally in the six fixed shell calls that inline the three steps plus the orchestrator's new commit call, each written out in full. In what form is the bounded retry written at each git write: a loop spelled out around each `git add` and `git commit` line in every call, a wrapper defined inside each call, or a helper shipped under `tools/` that runs the write and retries?

A git write can fail for reasons other than a lock, such as a hook refusing the commit or a pathspec matching no file, and repeating a failed write lands nothing. Does a write repeat on every non-zero exit, with the runner reading nothing of git's message, or only when git's message names the lock it could not take?
open-question.alternative: Every git write (`git add`, `git commit`) repeats on any non-zero exit, whatever its code or message. Nothing of git's output is read or matched, by the runner or by the call. Once the bound is spent, the last attempt's message passes on unchanged. This is the position the draft `ideas/milestones_addressed_by_path.md` takes. It is the simplest trigger to write at all seven sites and in the commit procedure's prose. It needs no captured stderr and no pattern that git's wording or locale could break, and it fits the plugin-wide convention that a runner never classifies an error's wording. A failed write lands nothing, so a repeat never commits twice. Every failure that is not about a lock waits out the whole retry window before it surfaces: a hook refusing the commit, nothing to commit, a commit pathspec matching no file (all exit 1), and a missing `git add` pathspec (exit 128). A refusing pre-commit hook runs once per attempt, so any side effects it has, such as formatting or stashing files, repeat. How long the wasted wait lasts depends on the attempt count and pause the Retry schedule question sets.

A write repeats only when git exits with 128, its fatal-error code, which is the code a held `index.lock` produces. Exit 1 passes on at once: a hook refusal, nothing to commit, or a commit pathspec matching no file. The exit status is the only thing tested, and no message text is read. It skips the retry for the common non-lock refusals: hooks, empty commits, and `git commit`'s pathspec miss. It still reads nothing of git's message, so it needs no captured stderr and no wording-dependent pattern, and a test of `$?` is as easy to write in a fixed call as any non-zero test. 128 is not specific to the lock. `git add` with a pathspec matching no file exits 128 (checked here with git 2.50.1), and so do other fatal errors, such as a permission refusal on `.git`, which Codex's read-only sandbox can produce. All of these still wait out the window. The rule also depends on an exit-code convention that git does not document as a contract for each failure.

A write repeats only when git's captured message names the index lock as held, matching the `Unable to create '….git/index.lock': File exists.` form. Every other failure passes on at once on its first attempt, ref-lock failures on `git commit` included, which are left to git's own default ref-lock wait. Only the one contention git does not wait on at all, the index lock, is retried. Every other refusal, including a missing pathspec or a sandbox's `Operation not permitted` on the same lock path, surfaces immediately with git's message, and a refusing hook runs exactly once. Each write's stderr has to be captured and matched against git's English wording, which a translated locale or a future git release could change. Wherever a runner follows the commit procedure by its own tool calls, the match becomes a reading of the message, which cuts against the convention that a runner never classifies an error's wording. Two runs committing to one branch at once can still fail on the ref lock or a moved HEAD after git's default tenth of a second. How the match is written depends on the form the Retry form in calls question chooses.

A write repeats only when git's captured message names a lock it could not take, either the index lock or a ref lock: the `Unable to create '….lock': File exists.` form for any lock file, or the `cannot lock ref` form, which also covers a branch moved by another run's commit. Every other failure passes on at once on its first attempt. This covers every contention two runs in one tree can produce at a write, including the commit's update of the shared branch ref, which git waits on for only a tenth of a second. Hooks, empty commits, missing pathspecs, and permission refusals still surface immediately and run once. It carries the widest pattern to keep correct against git's English wording, a broader dependence on message text than the index-only match, with the same tension against the convention that a runner never classifies an error's wording wherever the procedure is followed by hand. A `cannot lock ref` that comes from a genuinely broken ref is retried for nothing. How the match is written depends on the form the Retry form in calls question chooses.

open-question.question: `git add` and `git commit` take a pathspec from a file through `--pathspec-from-file`, which puts a floor of git 2.26 under a plugin that checks no git version today, while `git status` does not, and a shell read of the file into arguments needs no floor but splits the words itself. How does the orchestrator's one commit call read the recorded paths from the agent's file for its guard, its `git add`, and its commit, and if through git's own flag, where is the resulting git version floor checked or stated: the bootstrap's prerequisite check beside the Python one, the README prerequisite alone, or nowhere?
open-question.alternative: The orchestrator's commit call reads the path file through git's own flag: the guard is a dry-run `git add --dry-run --pathspec-from-file=<file>`, whose print is exactly the changed paths (an empty print meaning nothing to commit), then `git add --pathspec-from-file=<file>` and `git commit --pathspec-from-file=<file>`, so no shell code splits the file. The resulting git 2.26 floor is checked by `init-milestone-base-workflow`, its existing git step extended with a `git --version` comparison beside the Python one and a stop when the version is lower, and the README prerequisite sentence names 2.26 beside Python 3.9. Git parses the file line by line itself, so whitespace and odd characters in paths are handled with no shell splitting, and a too-old git is caught before any milestone exists, in the one place the plugin already checks its prerequisites, with the README and the check saying the same thing. The draft expects the next milestone to remove the bootstrap's checks, so the probe would land in a step about to go; the bootstrap runs once per project, so a later git downgrade or another contributor's machine is never re-checked; and it adds version parsing of strings such as `git version 2.39.3 (Apple Git-145)`, a new fixed stop line, and its row in the fixed-lines table.

The call reads the path file through git's own flag exactly as above (dry-run `add` from the file as the guard, then `add` and `commit` from the same file), and the git 2.26 floor is stated in the README prerequisite sentence alone; no skill checks the git version, and the README's statement that the bootstrap checks both prerequisites is reworded so it does not claim a version check. The requirement is written down where users read prerequisites at the cost of one sentence, with no new stop line, no version parsing, and nothing that depends on whether the bootstrap's checks survive the next milestone. Nothing enforces it: a user on git older than 2.26 (Ubuntu 18.04 ships 2.17, Debian 10 ships 2.20) first learns of it when the orchestrator's commit call fails with git's unknown-option message, after a task's work is already done and left uncommitted in the tree.

The call reads the path file through git's own flag as above, and the git 2.26 floor is checked where the flag is used: `complete-all-tasks` gains a precondition that runs `git --version` once per run, before its first dispatch, and stops on a fixed stop line of its own when the version is lower; the README prerequisite sentence states the floor beside Python 3.9, and the bootstrap is unchanged. The check sits in the only skill that needs the floor and runs on every invocation, so it catches an old git on any machine before any agent does task work, and it is untouched by whatever the next milestone does to the bootstrap. It makes `complete-all-tasks` the plugin's one skill with a git version check, adding a precondition step, version parsing, a new fixed stop line with its fixed-lines table row, and a probe on every run for a floor almost every installed git has cleared since 2020.

The call reads the path file through git's own flag as above, and the 2.26 floor is neither checked nor stated anywhere: the README keeps its unversioned git prerequisite and the bootstrap keeps its work-tree check alone, so an old git surfaces only as git's own error from the commit call. It costs no line of prose and no check anywhere, on the reasoning that 2.26 dates from March 2020 and any git that fails it reports the unknown option itself through the call's unredirected output. The plugin silently depends on a git version it never names, so a user on an older distribution's git gets a mid-run failure with no documented requirement to explain it, and a later contributor has no record that the floor exists.

The call reads the path file in the shell, line by line with `IFS= read -r`, into its argument list (the positional parameters, quoted as `"$@"`), and passes that list to the guard `git status --porcelain --`, to `git add --`, and to `git commit --` behind an explicit check that the list is not empty; git's file flag is not used, so no git version floor arises and nothing is checked or stated. It adds no git floor at all and keeps the guard in the commit procedure's own `git status --porcelain` form, while still taking each line as one path, so paths with spaces stay whole. A path list held in the shell runs against the committing invariant's wording that no path list is held in a shell variable and must behave identically under bash and zsh; and because a commit with no pathspec takes the whole index, the call needs its own empty-list check, more shell code in a fixed call a runner must copy exactly.

The call passes the file's contents as unquoted command substitution, `$(cat <file>)`, after `--` on the guard `git status --porcelain`, on `git add`, and on `git commit`, letting the shell split the paths on whitespace; git's file flag is not used, so no floor arises and nothing is checked or stated. It is the shortest form, one substitution per git line with no loop and no version requirement. A path holding a space or tab is split into two pathspecs that match nothing, so `git add` fails and the task's commit stops; bash also glob-expands the words while zsh does not, so the same call behaves differently per shell; and an empty file leaves `git commit` with no pathspec, committing the whole index, the very leak the milestone exists to close.

open-question.question: The orchestrator must find each task's path file in the scratch directory without the agent returning its name, and the alternatives agent's precedent derives its file name from the Short Title, so that a title holding a path separator fails the write and surfaces as a FAILED skip. Is the completion agent's path file one fixed name per run that each task's agent overwrites, or a name derived from the task title, one file per task?
open-question.alternative: One fixed file name per run, written literally in both the agent file and the orchestrator's commit call (for example `<scratch dir>/paths`). Each task's agent overwrites it with its own recorded paths, the orchestrator reads that one literal path after every DONE, and nothing moves or renames it between tasks, so at the end of the run it holds only the last task's list. No part of the name comes from the task title. No task title ever enters a file name, so no title fails the write (2 of the 468 task headings recorded in this repository hold a `/`, and two hold a double quote), and the commit call names one constant path with no per-task substitution or shell quoting of the title; because `complete-all-tasks` dispatches one task at a time and commits before the next dispatch, overwriting never collides within a run. A previous task's list stays at the same path when an agent returns DONE without writing one, so the orchestrator cannot tell an absent file from a stale one and would re-run its guard and commit over the previous task's paths, which under same-tree parallel runs may now hold another run's live edits committed under the wrong subject (how an absent or empty file is treated belongs to a sibling question); the scratch directory keeps no per-task record, and the scheme depends on the dispatch staying sequential.

One fixed file name per run that every agent writes, as in the overwritten form, but the orchestrator's commit call moves the file out of the way after reading it, into a `processed` subdirectory under a name the call makes unique (for example through `mktemp` inside that subdirectory), following the alternatives pass's move-into-processed precedent and deleting nothing. The fixed name is therefore absent whenever the next agent starts, and no part of either name comes from the task title. Keeps the title out of every file name, and so free of path-separator and quoting failures, while making an agent that wrote no list show as a missing file rather than a stale one, and leaving every task's list on disk for inspection. Adds a move and a uniqueness step to the orchestrator's one commit call, and the kept files carry no readable link to the task they came from; a move that fails after the commit leaves the stale file in place for the next task, and the scheme still depends on dispatch staying sequential.

One file per task directly inside the scratch directory, named by the task's `##` heading exactly as given plus a fixed extension (for example `<scratch dir>/<Task Title>.paths`), never shortened, slugged, or escaped, as the alternatives agent names its return; the orchestrator derives the path from the heading it already holds, and a title holding a path separator fails the write, which the agent reports as `FAILED` with no directory created to make it succeed. Files are never overwritten or moved, so the directory ends the run with one list per task. Reuses the one naming rule the plugin already has for a scratch-directory return, so agent file, orchestrator call, and the dispatch-prompt invariant read alike at both dispatch sites, each task's list stays on disk under its own readable name, and a task that wrote nothing shows as a missing file rather than a stale one. A legitimate task whose heading holds a `/` cannot complete under `complete-all-tasks` and ends the run on a `FAILED` after doing its work, since the list is written at the end of the task; and the orchestrator's commit call must carry the heading inside a quoted path, where a title's double quote, `$`, or backtick needs the same care the commit subject already does.

One directory per task inside the scratch directory, named by the task's `##` heading exactly as given (`<scratch dir>/<Task Title>/`), holding the path list under a fixed file name, the layout the draft's second milestone describes for the commit message and the recorded paths together; the agent creates the directory and writes the list into it, a title holding a path separator is stated to fail as a `FAILED`, and nothing is overwritten or moved. Lands the layout the draft's next milestone already plans, so adding the commit-message file there adds one file beside the list rather than renaming this milestone's return, while keeping per-task records and making a missing list detectable. Asks the agent for a directory creation as well as a write for one file this milestone, and a separator in the title no longer fails on its own (a parent-creating `mkdir` or write tool builds nested directories and succeeds), so the failure holds only by the agent obeying a stated rule; it carries the exact-title form's quoting cost and its `FAILED` for headings holding a `/`.

One file per task named by a fixed transform of the task's `##` heading (for example path separators and shell-special characters replaced, the rest kept) plus a fixed extension, the transform stated once and applied identically by the agent when writing and by the orchestrator when reading; no title fails the write, and nothing is overwritten or moved. Every task can complete whatever its heading holds, while keeping one readable, detectable file per task and keeping shell-special characters out of the path the commit call quotes. The transform must be stated so both runners apply it identically, and a drift between the agent file and the orchestrator silently loses a task's list; two headings that differ only in replaced characters map to one name although the task-list tool keeps them distinct, and it departs from the alternatives agent's explicit never-slug rule, giving the plugin two naming rules for scratch-directory returns.

The orchestrator chooses each task's file name itself, free of the title (for example the task's ordinal in the run), and passes it to the agent as one more fixed line in the dispatch prompt (or passes the full file path in place of the bare scratch directory); the agent writes exactly the path it was given, and nothing is overwritten or moved. No title character can break the name or the commit call's quoting, each task still gets its own file so a missing list is detectable, and the agent applies no naming rule of its own. Adds a per-dispatch value the orchestrator must generate and hold across loop iterations, and grows the two-line prompt fence (and the Antigravity on-demand test's prompt helper) beyond the goal's scratch-directory line, against the dispatch-prompt rule's preference for the smallest prompt; the kept files carry no readable link to their task.

open-question.question: The move the agent runs edits the milestone's TASKS_TODO.md and TASKS_DONE.md on its behalf, and the orchestrator already holds the milestone directory from its own resolution, while the draft's reason for the file is that the orchestrator holds no path and types none. Does the agent's path file list the two task files beside the paths it created or edited, or does the orchestrator add them to its commit call from the directory it holds?

Today a DONE with nothing staged is a no-op the whole-index guard absorbs; once the change set travels as a file, an absent or empty file after DONE is a distinct condition, an agent that completed the task but wrote no path list, which a guard on the file's paths cannot tell from a task that changed nothing. When an agent returns DONE and its path file is absent or empty, does the orchestrator take the task as having produced no committable change, or stop the run on a fixed stop line of its own?

The orchestrator's no-op line `Task run committed nothing — no task staged a change.` names staging, which the agent no longer does, and a fixed line is a contract harnesses match across versions, changing only together with its row in the fixed-lines table. Does the line keep its wording unchanged, or is it reworded to stop naming the retired mechanism?
open-question.alternative: The no-op line stays byte-for-byte `Task run committed nothing — no task staged a change.`, in `core/skills/complete-all-tasks/SKILL.md` and in its row of `docs/skill-reference.md`'s `## Fixed console lines` table alike. Only the prose around it changes: the sentence introducing the line, and the step-2c guard it summarizes, are rewritten for the commit-from-file call, while the printed line itself still says "staged". No harness matching the line across versions breaks, and nothing in the fixed-lines table, `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py`, or any host tree needs touching for it. That keeps the contract the table exists to provide, under which a line changes only when it has to. The line names a mechanism the milestone retires. Once the agent stops staging, "no task staged a change" describes nothing that happens in the run. A reader or harness author would take it at face value, and it would disagree with the reworded `docs/workflow.md`, `docs/skill-reference.md`, and the committing invariant, which will no longer say anything is staged by the agent.

The line keeps its opening clause `Task run committed nothing —` and only the reason after the dash is reworded to name no git or hand-off mechanism, for example `Task run committed nothing — no task changed a file.` The reworded line replaces the old one in `complete-all-tasks` and in its fixed-lines table row in the same change, and `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` then checks the new text in every host tree. The line stops naming the retired mechanism and names none to replace it, so it survives the draft's later milestones changing how a change set travels again. Keeping the prefix lets a harness that matches on the clause before the dash keep working. This matches the shape of sibling no-op lines such as `complete-task`'s `No task completed — no file changed.` Any harness matching the whole line, which is the form the table and the test define, breaks on upgrade and has to update its match. A one-time contract change is spent on wording alone, for a condition that is rarely if ever reached, because a successful move always changes the two task files.

The line is reworded to name the mechanism that replaces staging: the paths each agent writes to its file in the run's scratch directory. An example is `Task run committed nothing — no task recorded a changed path.` It is changed together with its fixed-lines table row and checked by `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` as in any rewording. It says exactly what the orchestrator's guard checks under the new design, so the line keeps describing the run's real mechanism the way the old one did when it was written. A reader who sees it knows to look at the agents' path files, not at the index. It breaks whole-line harness matches just as any rewording does, and it ties the line to a mechanism again, so a later change to how the change set travels would force another rewording. Its accuracy also depends on the sibling questions on whether the path file lists the task files and on how a missing or empty path file is handled. If a missing file is treated as no committable change, "recorded" no longer holds for that case.

The committed-nothing condition, its fixed line, and its row in the fixed-lines table are removed. A run whose tasks all returned `DONE` always ends on `All tasks completed.`, and step 2c's per-task guard either stays as a silent skip or goes with the line. `tests/test_fixed_console_lines.py` needs no change of its own, because it checks only the rows the table lists. It removes a line describing a condition the new commit call cannot reach. Every `DONE` follows a successful `move`, which changes `TASKS_TODO.md` and `TASKS_DONE.md`, and those files reach the commit one way or another, so a whole run with nothing committed cannot happen. The plugin then stops promising harnesses an outcome that never occurs, and the stale wording question goes away with it. A harness matching the line loses it with no replacement, and an outcome that was listed simply disappears from the contract. Whether the condition is truly unreachable depends on the sibling questions on whether the task files reach the commit through the path file or from the orchestrator's own directory, and on what a missing or empty path file after `DONE` means. If the line is retired and a reachable case is left, the run would print the success line over a run that committed nothing.

open-question.question: The goal's one test runs two milestones' tasks in parallel in one repository and asserts each commit carries only its own paths, but a test dispatches no agent, so it must run a fixed call extracted from the rendered tree the way the sweep's test does. Which call does the test run concurrently for its two milestones: the orchestrator's commit-from-file call fed by path files the test writes, the inline complete-task skill's chained move-and-commit call, or both?

Two calls started together in one repository may or may not collide on `.git/index.lock`, so the parallel test exercises the retry only by chance, while a test can hold the lock itself and release it within the retry window. Is the lock retry tested deterministically that way, or left to the parallel test's race and otherwise untested?

The `environment`, `repo`, `git`, and `run_call` helpers that build an isolated git repository live inside `tests/test_sweep_batched_call.py`, `tests/conftest.py` carries no git fixture, and the suite's convention is one flat file per concern. Does the new parallel test share those helpers by moving them into `tests/conftest.py`, or carry its own copies?

The goal makes several complete-all-tasks runs able to share one working tree, but the scope gate that keeps two runs' cores apart belongs to a later milestone, and today's docs say the tree is clean after each skill (design claim 12) and that tasks run one at a time (claim 9). Do the docs present same-tree parallel runs as a supported way of using the plugin in this release, with a chain on the ways-of-using page and the claims reworded, or record only the commit mechanism and leave the capability unstated until the gate lands?
open-question.alternative: The docs present same-tree parallel completion runs as supported in this release. `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` gains a chain that starts two `complete-all-tasks --milestone <milestone_id>` lines together in one working tree. Design claim 9 is reworded to one task at a time within a milestone, with several milestones' runs allowed side by side. Claim 12's "the work tree is clean after each skill" is reworded to per-commit hygiene: each commit records only its own paths, and the tree is clean once no other run is live. The chain's prose states the interim condition that, until the scope gate lands, the operator picks milestones whose work touches disjoint files. `docs/workflow.md` and the invariants record the pathspec, the retry, and the commit-from-file mechanism. The capability the milestone exists to deliver becomes visible and usable as soon as it ships, and the goal's own parallel test backs the claim. The docs also stop saying things that are false once two runs share a tree. The docs offer a recipe for parallel execution while the safeguard that keeps two runs' cores apart does not exist yet, so the only thing keeping the runs apart is a sentence the operator may skip. The draft's third milestone then rewrites claim 9 and the chain again around the gate, which means two edits of one contract.

The docs state same-tree parallel completion runs as supported, with no copy-paste chain. Claims 9 and 12 are reworded as in a full-support release: one task at a time within a milestone, and per-commit hygiene in place of a clean tree after each skill. One prose passage, in `docs/workflow.md` or the claims, says several milestones' `complete-all-tasks` runs may share one tree and that, until the scope gate lands, the operator keeps their work on disjoint files. `docs/ways-of-using-cairn.md` gains no chain. The mechanism is recorded as in every option. The claims say what is true of the release, and the capability is documented for anyone who reads for it, without the ways-of-using page's ready-to-run recipe inviting headless users into an ungated parallel run. It is a half-measure. A capability declared supported but given no chain on the page that collects the plugin's supported headless uses reads as hesitant, and the claim-9 rewording still has to be redone when the gate lands.

The docs cover only the same-tree concurrency they already describe. They record the pathspec, retry, and commit-from-file mechanism and state that the existing "Preparing the next milestone while the current one runs" chain no longer leaks a completion agent's files into the sweep's or a pass's commit. Claim 12 is reworded to per-commit hygiene, since a preparation run beside a live completion run already leaves the tree dirty. Claim 9 stays as written. Two `complete-all-tasks` runs in one tree are left unstated, and no new chain is added. It tells users the one parallel use the plugin already documents is now safe, and fixes claim 12 where it is already false today, without promising ungated parallel execution before the gate's milestone can back it. The milestone's headline purpose, several completion runs in one tree, ships with its mechanism and test but no user-facing statement. Claim 9 then sits beside a working capability it denies until the gate's milestone rewrites it.

The docs record only the commit mechanism: the pathspec commit, the bounded retry, the agent's path file, and the orchestrator's commit-from-file. These go into `docs/workflow.md` `## How skills commit`, the `docs/skill-reference.md` entries, and the committing and return-contract invariants. Claim 12 changes only its staging wording, so the agent no longer stages, and keeps its clean-tree sentence. Claim 9 is untouched. No chain is added, and parallel runs are not mentioned. The capability is first stated when the gate lands. It is the smallest docs change. Every claim the docs make, and every chain they offer, keeps resting on a safeguard that exists, and the capability is described once, together with the gate that bounds it, with no interim wording to retire. The docs say nothing about a capability the release really has and its test exercises, and claim 12's clean-tree sentence stays false for the preparation chain the ways-of-using page already offers. A user who finds parallel runs on their own has no stated condition for doing it safely.

The docs record the commit mechanism, as in a mechanism-only release, and add an explicit statement, in claim 9 or beside the ways-of-using page's execution chain, that running two `complete-all-tasks` runs in one working tree is not supported until the scope gate lands. Claim 9 otherwise stands, claim 12 changes only its staging wording, and no chain is added. Nobody mistakes the new commit mechanism for permission to run ungated parallel execution. The docs keep the one-at-a-time promise and say plainly where its boundary lies until the gate exists. It disclaims the exact capability the milestone builds and tests, which leaves a negative statement in the docs that the gate's milestone must delete. It also discourages a use that is safe for milestones whose work is disjoint.
